summary: This standards-track memo explains how TCP and UDP can use IPv6 jumbograms, packets larger than the usual 16-bit limit allows. It describes simple changes for UDP and for TCP's MSS option and Urgent field. It was replaced by RFC 2675.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2147 explains how TCP and UDP can work with IPv6 jumbograms, which are larger than 65,535 bytes. It updates RFC 1883 and was later replaced by RFC 2675.

subtitle: Changes that let TCP and UDP use IPv6 jumbograms

tldr.problem: IPv6 supports jumbograms larger than 65,535 bytes, but UDP's length field and TCP's MSS and Urgent fields are limited by 16-bit values.
tldr.mechanism: UDP uses a zero length field to signal that the true length comes from the IPv6 jumbo payload information; TCP treats an MSS value of 65,535 as infinity and handles long urgent offsets by splitting data.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2147 updates RFC 1883 and was later replaced by RFC 2675.

sections.title: Making Room for Jumbograms
sections.content:
IPv6 supports datagrams longer than 65,535 bytes using the Jumbo Payload hop-by-hop option. UDP has a 16-bit length field, and TCP's negotiated Maximum Segment Size (MSS) and Urgent Pointer are also constrained by 16-bit values.

This RFC describes changes that allow TCP and UDP to use IPv6 jumbograms without changing the size of those fields.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 can carry a packet larger than the size represented by some TCP and UDP fields. This RFC explains how the protocols handle those larger packets.

sections.title: UDP Length and TCP MSS
sections.content:
When the UDP header plus data is longer than 65,535 bytes, the sender sets the UDP length field to zero. The receiver uses the length in the IPv6 jumbo payload option, adjusted for extension headers between the IPv6 and UDP headers, to determine the UDP packet's length. The UDP checksum still uses the true length, not zero.

For TCP, if the directly attached interface MTU is greater than 65,535, the sender advertises an MSS of 65,535. The receiver treats that value as infinity and uses MTU discovery, starting with the outgoing interface MTU, to find the actual MSS.
sections.plainLanguage: For a long UDP packet, zero means to get the real length from IPv6. For TCP, an MSS of 65,535 means MTU discovery will determine the actual size.

sections.title: TCP Urgent Data
sections.content:
The TCP Urgent Pointer cannot directly reference data beyond 65,535 bytes. If an urgent offset is greater than 65,535 and falls within the TCP data, the sender splits the packet into two pieces. It sets the first piece's Urgent field to 65,535 to indicate that the urgent data is beyond that piece, then sends the second piece with the Urgent field set normally.

When a receiver sees the URG bit and an Urgent field of 65,535, it calculates the urgent pointer using the TCP data length rather than that field value. The RFC says there are no known security issues involved in these changes.
sections.plainLanguage: If urgent data lies too far ahead for the pointer field, TCP divides the data. The first piece signals that the urgent point is beyond it, and the next piece carries the normal pointer.
